passage: After the village fair in Bikaner, Ojas, five, threw himself on the ground because his father Trisha had said no to a fourth balloon. He screamed, kicking, and dust rose. Trisha squatted beside him, hands loose, not speaking. When the screaming eased, Ojas sobbed, "You said... you said I could have it... at the start!" Trisha said, "You're sad and cross because you wanted more. The balloons are finished for today, but we can walk to see the camels." Ojas wiped his nose and, still hiccuping, took his father's hand.

qa.q: Why did Ojas throw himself on the ground?
qa.a: His father had said no to a fourth balloon.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he cried and explained what went wrong?
qa.a: He felt sad and cross because he wanted another balloon, and he thought he was told he could have it. Feelings this big can outrun his words.

qa.q: What did Trisha do that worked well?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named the feeling and set a kind limit with the offer of camels, without punishing the tears.

qa.q: How might Trisha feel while Ojas screams and kicks in the dust?
qa.a: Trisha seems calm and patient, squatting beside him with loose hands and waiting until the screaming eases before naming his feelings.

grounding: A preschooler wails in a tantrum then cries while explaining, and a calm adult names the feeling and sets a kind limit.

passage: In their kitchen in Enugu, Chidi, four, wailed when his older sister Paulo took the last biscuit. His face was red and tears rolled. "It's mine!" Paulo froze. Their father knelt down. "You're really upset." Chidi kept crying, then said, wetly, "She always... gets the big one." "So you feel it's unfair," said their father. "We can fix it. You're going to choose which biscuit you'd like tomorrow, first." Chidi sniffed. "Promise?" Their father nodded.

qa.q: What did Paulo take?
qa.a: Paulo took the last biscuit.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling when he said "She always... gets the big one"?
qa.a: He felt it was unfair and was hurt and angry. The words came out while he was still crying, so he was probably still very upset.

qa.q: What could their father do next to help both children?
qa.a: He can keep his promise about choosing first and make sure Paulo also feels heard.

qa.q: How might Paulo feel after freezing and hearing Chidi?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and a little guilty, and may want to make it right.

grounding: A preschooler wails then cries while explaining what went wrong, and a calm adult names the emotion and offers a fix.

passage: At the art club, Ankita's painting fell into the water tray. She wailed, a high, loud cry, and flung her brush across the table. Harish, the art teacher, didn't raise his voice. He crouched beside her. “You're so sad. Your painting got wet.” Ankita sobbed harder. “It… was… the best… one… and the sun… went… all… runny!” “I hear you. You can cry, but brushes stay on the table.” She nodded between sobs, and he helped her lay the painting in the sun to dry.

qa.q: Where did Ankita's painting fall?
qa.a: Into the water tray.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she wailed and threw her brush?
qa.a: She was very sad and frustrated that her best painting was ruined, and the feeling was bigger than her words at first.

qa.q: How did Harish set a kind limit?
qa.a: He named her sadness and said she could cry, but brushes stay on the table, then helped her dry the painting.

qa.q: How might the other children see Ankita's wail?
qa.a: They might be startled by the loud cry and the flying brush, and calmed when Harish stayed steady.

grounding: A preschooler wails in a tantrum, then cries while explaining, and a calm teacher names the feeling and sets a kind limit.

passage: I'm Jasleen, from the seventh floor. In the lift today, Zubin's mother pressed the button before he could. Zubin let out a huge wail and kicked the lift door. His mother stayed very calm. She said, “You wanted to press it. You're so sad. But we don't kick doors.” Zubin cried, “I… always… press… it!” in gasps. She said, “You can press it on the way down.” I couldn't tell if he heard, but by the fourth floor his cries were hiccups.

qa.q: What did Zubin kick?
qa.a: The lift door.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when he wailed?
qa.a: He was very upset and frustrated that he missed pressing the button, and his words came out in gasps because the feeling was too big.

qa.q: What did Zubin's mother do that works better than punishing tears?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named the feeling, set a kind limit about kicking and offered a way forward.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt watching in the small lift?
qa.a: Jasleen might have felt a bit awkward in the small space, but noticed and admired the mother's calm.

grounding: A neighbour observes a preschooler wail in the lift, then cry while explaining, while his mother stays calm and sets a kind limit.

passage:
Sunday: Afreen wailed when her tower fell. Vandana, her mother, snapped, “Stop crying or no park!” Afreen screamed louder and threw a block.
Tuesday: The tower fell again. This time Vandana sat down beside her. “You're so upset. It fell down.” Afreen sobbed, “It was… tall… and… Cat… knocked it!” Vandana said, “That's frustrating. Blocks stay on the floor, though.”
Thursday: When it fell, Afreen cried for a minute, then said, “Cat did it again,” and started building.

qa.q: Who knocked the tower down on Tuesday?
qa.a: The cat.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling on Tuesday as she sobbed and explained?
qa.a: She was upset and frustrated that her tall tower fell, and her words came slowly through the tears.

qa.q: What changed between Sunday and Tuesday that helped?
qa.a: Vandana stopped threatening and instead stayed calm, named the feeling and set a kind limit about throwing blocks.

qa.q: How might Vandana feel on Thursday when Afreen recovers quickly?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and encouraged that staying calm works better than punishing tears.

grounding: Over a week, a mother learns that staying calm and naming feelings helps her preschooler's tantrums better than punishing tears.

passage:
The rain came down so hard that Kalyani's paper boat turned to mush in the drain before it sailed. She dropped onto the wet step and wailed, kicking one sandal off into the puddle.

Ayesha crouched beside her under the umbrella. "You're so sad. Your boat got ruined. You can cry. But we keep sandals on our feet."

Kalyani sobbed and pulled the sandal back on. "I... made it... with Nani... and it didn't even... go!"

"You made it with Nani, and it didn't get a turn." Ayesha rubbed her back. "Let's make another when the rain slows."

qa.q: What happened to Kalyani's paper boat?
qa.a: It turned to mush in the drain before it sailed.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she wailed and kicked off her sandal?
qa.a: She was most likely very sad and disappointed that the boat she made with Nani was ruined. Her broken, sobbing words show the feeling was bigger than her words at first.

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that worked better than punishing the tears?
qa.a: She stayed calm, named the sadness, allowed the crying, set a kind limit about the sandals, and offered to make another boat.

qa.q: What would change if Ayesha had said, "Stop crying, it's only paper"?
qa.a: Kalyani would probably have cried harder or hidden her sadness, and might not have explained what the boat meant to her.

grounding: It shows a preschooler wailing in a tantrum and then crying while explaining, with a calm adult naming the feeling and setting a kind limit.
